food.text: The annual market of Souk Okaz in the Hejaz ran for twenty-one days each year before the Hajj pilgrimage and operated from about 542 to 726 CE. Sitting on the Spice Route through western Arabia, it grew in the sixth century partly because Byzantine-Persian wars made it harder for Mediterranean traders to reach Mesopotamian trade routes.

Arabia's food economy varied sharply by region. South and eastern Arabia relied on dams, floodwater diversion, terraces and wells for farming, while central Arabia's oases grew date palms and cereals alongside camels, sheep and goats, and northern and western oasis towns linked into caravan routes and seasonal markets.

The early diet of Eastern Arabia centred on dates, wheat, barley, rice and meat, with a heavy emphasis on yogurt products such as leben, a yogurt without butterfat. Many cooking techniques came from ancient Persia and were carried forward by Persians during the Sassanid Dynasty.

Early Hanafi scholars, like the Mu'tazila, held that intoxication was unlawful but restricted khamr to the fermented juice of grapes, or of grapes and dates. Alcohol from honey, barley, wheat and millet, such as beer, whisky or vodka, was permitted according to some minor faction of followers of Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, though all grape alcohol was banned absolutely. Hanafi jurists punished drinking grape wine even for "a drop", but for non-grape intoxicants only drunkenness counted, defined by Ibn Nujaym as not knowing the difference between a man and a woman or the earth from the sky. Hanafis traced their view back to Umar (d.644) and Abdullah ibn Masud (c.653).
Souk Okaz was not the only seasonal fair of its kind. It competed with two other markets, Majanna and Dhu'l-Majaz, both held near Mecca at the same time of year during the pilgrimage season.
Taif and Mecca were both pilgrimage resorts with close trading ties between their people. Alongside commerce, the people of Taif combined farming and fruit-growing as part of their livelihood.

During the early Middle Ages, Greek fleets tried to challenge Arab control of maritime trade between India and Egypt, but Arab trade persisted while Greek naval trade dwindled. Key harbors included Al-Ubulla, Gerrha and Sohar in the east and Mocha, Qani and Aden in the south.

Okaz lost importance after the rise of Islam, as the expanding caliphate opened new trade routes and changed the roles of Arabian tribes. The market met its end when Kharijites sacked and destroyed it in 725 to 726 CE.

art.text: The Great Mosque of Sanaa in Yemen is said to have been founded around 633 CE, making it one of the oldest mosques in the world. It was built in part from spolia taken from the Himyarite-era Ghumdan Palace and the Axumite Christian Church of al-Qalis, both of which once stood on the site.

When Muhammad conquered Mecca in 630 CE, one report says there were 360 idols around the Kaaba and that he struck them with a stick, saying "Truth has come and Falsehood has vanished." His first action was to remove the statues and images from the Kaaba, and it is said the 360 idols were destroyed. According to reports collected by Ibn Ishaq and al-Azraqi, he spared a painting of Mary and Jesus and a fresco of Ibrahim. Al-Azraqi also has him say "May Allah kill those representing him as a venerable old man casting arrows in divination" about the picture of Ibrahim, and order every picture erased except that of Maryam.

By the second half of the 6th century CE, the Islamic expansion had begun to displace the older artistic traditions of ancient South Arabia, centred on the kingdoms of the Sabaeans and Himyar, with early Islamic art. For centuries before this, sculptors there had worked mainly in bronze, limestone, and occasionally gold and silver.

The Kaaba was severely damaged by fire on 31 October 683 CE, during the first siege of Mecca in the war between the Umayyads and 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. In the second siege, in 692, the Umayyad army under al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf bombarded the Kaaba with stones. The city fell and 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr died. In 693 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan had the remnants razed and rebuilt it, and its basic shape has not changed since, about six decades after Muhammad had removed the statues and images from inside it.

The Umayyad caliph al-Walid I expanded the Great Mosque of Sanaa between 705 and 715 CE, in the early 8th century. This is recorded as one of the earliest renovations made to the mosque since its founding.

An inscription found in the courtyard of the Great Mosque of Sanaa has been dated to 753 CE, placing it in the Abbasid period. It stands as evidence that the mosque continued to be worked on after the earlier Umayyad expansion.
In the early 9th century, a minaret was added to the east side of the Great Mosque of Sanaa. This addition came long after the mosque's founding and its Umayyad-era expansion under al-Walid I.

In the year 911 CE, the Karmatis invaded Sanaa and damaged the Great Mosque there. By that point the building had already passed through Umayyad expansion and Abbasid-era renovation over nearly two centuries.

war.text: Arabia in late antiquity saw the rise of imperial proxy warfare involving the Byzantine and Sasanian empires. That era ended quickly when Muhammad established the first Islamic state in Medina in 622. The peninsula was conquered and politically unified shortly after his death, in the 630s.

After Muhammad died in 632, his followers expanded Muslim rule far beyond Arabia. In a matter of decades they conquered territory from the Iberian Peninsula in the west to parts of Central and South Asia in the east. Arabia itself became a more politically peripheral region.

Himyar's collapse in the sixth century had no single cause. Turbulent events included the violent coup of Dhu Nuwas, the massacre of the Christian community of Najran, the Aksumite conquest of Himyar, and a rebellion of Ethiopian soldiers in South Arabia against Aksum. Epidemic and climate played a part too: an inscription (CIH 541) from the 550s indicates that the Plague of Justinian struck South Arabia, and severe droughts ran from 500 to 530 CE.

When the Sasanian Persian ruler Khosrow I sent help to depose the king of Yemen, the war culminated in the Siege of Sanaa. Sasanian forces captured the capital of Aksumite Yemen. The Persian commander Wahrez then placed Ma'adi Yakrib on the Himyarite throne as a Sasanian vassal.

Arab leaders in the north fought and bargained between two empires. The Jafnids became major Roman-allied leaders in Syria and Arabia, while the Nasrids, or Lakhmids of Al-Hira, played a comparable role for the Sasanians. Neither was a passive client: they held broad independent powers.

After the Conquest of Mecca, Muhammad learned that the Hawazin confederation was readying an army twice as strong as his own force. The Thaqif of Ta'if joined them. Both tribes were defeated in the Battle of Hunayn.

Around the early sixth century, the Himyarite prince Dhu Nuwas seized power by killing the Aksumite garrison in Zafār. His campaign against the Ethiopian guards and their Christian allies killed between 11,500 and 14,000 people and took a similar number of prisoners. He then massacred the Christian community of Najran, and an inscription describes burning a church and slaughtering Abyssinians, claiming thousands of deaths and prisoners. The Kingdom of Aksum struck back and conquered Himyar in 525-530, ending its independence and deposing Dhu Nuwas. Christianity became the main religion after the Aksumite conquest in 530 CE, and an Aksumite-backed regime ruled until Sasanian intervention brought Yemen under Sasanian influence in 575 or 578.

By the 550s and 560s Himyar's decline was complete, as it faced military incursions from Central and Northwest Arabia and local insurrections. This followed the Plague of Justinian, which an inscription (CIH 541) from the 550s shows struck South Arabia, and severe droughts from 500 to 530 CE. The final Himyarite inscription was recorded in 559 CE, and the Marib Dam broke down over the 570s.

After the battle of Uhud, Abu Sufyan tried to raise a more powerful army. He won over the great nomadic tribes north and east of Medina with propaganda about Muhammad's weakness, promises of treasure, memories of Quraysh prestige, and straight bribes.

Muhammad launched the Expedition of Tabuk against the Byzantine Empire and their Ghassanid allies in the north. He did not make contact with hostile forces there, but he received the submission of some local chiefs. Afterwards the Banu Thaqif and other Bedouins also submitted.

After his war with King Aidug, the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas turned on the Christian city of Najran, a dependency of his kingdom. After its surrender, he offered the citizens a choice between embracing Judaism under coercion and being put to death. When they refused to renounce their faith, he executed their chief, Harith ibn Kaleb, and three hundred and forty chosen men. The war with Aidug had itself begun after Dhu Nuwas put Byzantine merchants to death, burning them in large pits, which earned him the title "King of the burning pit".
Following the battle of Badr, Muhammad made mutual-aid alliances with a number of Bedouin tribes. The purpose was to protect his community from attacks from the northern part of Hejaz.

literature.text: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry was composed roughly between 540 and 620 AD. The poets did not write their works down. The poems were transmitted orally and only codified into collections by later authors, beginning in the eighth century.

Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry was composed roughly between 540 and 620 AD, yet the poets themselves did not write it down. It was passed on orally and only later gathered into collections by authors, beginning in the eighth century.

Pre-Islamic poetry is a major source for the classical Arabic language, both in grammar and vocabulary. It also serves as a record of the political and cultural life of the time in which it was created.

Arabic became a written language only gradually. Before the fully developed Arabic script, it was written in several scripts, including Nabataean, North Arabian, South Arabian, and occasionally Greek.

The first extant written collection containing pre-Islamic poems was made by al-Mufaddal ad-Dabbi, who died after 780 AD. It held 126 poems and came to be known as the Mufaddaliyyat. It appears to have been composed as a teaching text for the Abbasid family.

The second major surviving collection of pre-Islamic poetry was the Asma'iyyat, compiled by the grammarian al-Asma'i, who died in 828. About 69 percent of its poems are Najdi, 17 percent southern Hijazi, and 11 percent Yemeni.

Poetry was first distinguished into Islamic and pre-Islamic by Hammad al-Rawiya, who died in 772. In Abbasid times, literary critics then debated whether contemporary or pre-Islamic poetry was the better of the two.

Most pre-Islamic poetry originated in the Najd, with only a minority coming from the Hejaz. In al-Mufaddal's collection, 78 of 126 poems, or 62 percent, come from Najdi or Iraqi tribes, and only 2 are from the Quraysh.

Adi ibn Zayd was a prominent Christian Arab poet stationed in al-Hira. In one famous, lengthy poem he swore by "the lord of Mecca and of the cross" and compared himself to a monk in his prayers. He also composed a poem on the creation of the world.

Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry suggests that its authors were monotheists or at least henotheists. It also hints at the existence of gentile monotheists, people who followed neither Christianity nor Judaism.

The poet Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur wrote of "the letters of two Jews from Taymāʾ or the people of Madyan on their parchments which they recite with accomplishment." His verse shows pre-Islamic Arabian poetry referring to Jewish written material.
Imru' al-Qais, the most prominent of the pre-Islamic poets, once mentioned Christian writings. He described something as "like a line of writing in the books of monks".
Both al-Mufaddal and al-Asma'i wrote numerous other works across a wide range of subjects. These included lexicography, phonetics, and Arabian topography.

The eighth-century Book of Idols by Hisham ibn al-Kalbi is a Muslim-era source that depicts pre-Islamic Arabia as dominated by polytheistic practices. Such writings portray a sudden rupture brought about by the coming of Muhammad.

science.text: A high-resolution hydroclimate study from northern Oman and related regional records indicates severe and persistent droughts in the early sixth century, especially between about 500 and 530 CE. Scientists reading this climate evidence argue that it helps explain how strained South Arabia was before the Himyarite kingdom's decline.
South Arabia depended heavily on water management. Himyarite power rested partly on irrigated and rain-fed agriculture, terraced fields, and the upkeep of dams and water systems.

The collapse of the Himyarite polity in the sixth century had no single cause. Political turmoil came first: the violent coup of Dhu Nuwas, the massacre of the Christian community of Najran, the Aksumite conquest of Himyar, and a rebellion of Ethiopian soldiers against Aksum. Epidemic and climatological factors added to it, including severe droughts from 500 to 530 CE, and the effects were most severe in the South, especially the Southwest. By the 550s and 560s Himyar also faced military incursions and local insurrections.

One inscription, CIH 541, from the 550s indicates that the Plague of Justinian struck South Arabia. It is evidence that an epidemic reached the region while the Himyarite kingdom was already in trouble.

Around the mid-6th century, the Late Antique Little Ice Age added to the pressures on South Arabia. It came on top of the earlier droughts of 500 to 530 CE and the plague, and its effects were most severe in the Southwest.

The breakdown of the Marib Dam over the course of the 570s is taken as a sign that the traditional order had collapsed. This great irrigation structure had once supported agriculture in the south. Its failure came after the Himyarite decline was completed by the 550s and 560s.

politics.text: Muhammad was born in Mecca in about 570 and first began preaching there in 610. He migrated to Medina in 622, and from there he and his companions united the tribes of Arabia under the banner of Islam. The result was the first Islamic state, a single Arab Muslim religious polity in the Arabian Peninsula.

In the early seventh century, Muhammad established the first Islamic state in Medina in 622. After his death in the 630s, the peninsula was conquered and politically unified shortly afterward. The pre-Islamic period closed quickly.

Arab dynasties originating from modern-day Saudi Arabia founded the Rashidun (632 to 661), Umayyad (661 to 750), Abbasid (750 to 1517) and Fatimid (909 to 1171) caliphates. They also founded numerous other dynasties in Asia, Africa and Europe.

The Kingdom of Himyar dominated South Arabia for centuries, but its polity unravelled during the sixth century and experienced a societal collapse. The violent coup of Dhu Nuwas, the massacre of the Christian community of Najran, the Aksumite conquest and a rebellion of Ethiopian soldiers all struck in rapid succession. An inscription (CIH 541) from the 550s shows that the Plague of Justinian struck South Arabia, and severe droughts ran from 500 to 530 CE. The last Himyarite inscription was recorded in 559 CE.

The Ziyadid dynasty ruled western Yemen from 819 until 1018 from the new city of Zabid. Muhammad was appointed amir of Yemen by al-Ma'mun and recognized Abbasid overlordship. It was the first dynasty to hold the Yemeni lowland after Islam arrived.

The Jewish king Dhu Nuwas, who had taken power in a violent coup, massacred the Christian community of Najran. In response, Kaleb, the Christian king of the Kingdom of Aksum, invaded and annexed Himyar. Ethiopian soldiers later rebelled against Aksum in South Arabia.

Himyar was ruled by an Aksumite-backed regime after the Aksumite invasion. Sasanian forces under Wahrez then captured Sanaa and placed Ma'adi Yakrib on the throne as a Sasanian vassal. In 575 or 578 Ma'adi Yakrib was killed by Aksumite servants, the war resumed, and Wahrez led another army of 8000 that ended Aksumite overlordship and brought Yemen under the influence of the Sasanian Empire. Native Christian kings had ruled Himyar from 500 CE to 521 or 522 CE.

The Hujrid dynasty ruled in central Arabia as clients of Himyar while dealing with Byzantium and Persia. Al-Harith negotiated directly with the Byzantine emperor Anastasius. He was killed in 528 CE by the Lakhmid ruler al-Mundhir.

The Yufirids established an independent state in San'a in 847. In 904 the Isma'ilis under Ibn Hawshab and Ali ibn al-Fadl al-Jayshani invaded Sana'a, and the Yufirid emir As'ad ibn Ibrahim retreated to Al-Jawf. Between 904 and 913, Sana'a was conquered no less than 20 times by Isma'ilis and Yufirids, and As'ad ibn Ibrahim regained it in 915. Yemen was in turmoil as the city became a battlefield for three dynasties and independent tribes. Zabid itself was sacked by the sectarian Qarmatians in 904.

Christianity was the religion shared by the Jafnids and the Romans, and it enabled their alliance to develop. Their counterparts, the Nasrids or Lakhmids of Al-Hira, played a similar role for the Sasanian side, though with different religious and political strategies.

At its largest, Himyar conquered much of the Arabian Peninsula, reaching lower Iraq. This seems to have happened around the mid-fifth century and again in the mid-sixth century, during the reign of Abraha.

After the mid-sixth century the Hujrids fade from the historical record. Roman sources stop mentioning them as the Jafnid dynasty became Rome's preferred Arab allies. The Nasrids also grew more influential in central Arabia.

In 866 the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'in came to a violent end. After that, the second Ziyadid ruler, Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, kept the tax revenues for himself and adopted royal trappings, as Abbasid rule in Arabia declined. He nevertheless continued reciting the khutba in the name of the Abbasids.

The Hujrid princess Hind married a Lakhmid king and lived in al-Hira, where she built a monastery. Its inscription calls her the daughter of kings and hopes her son will have strength to establish justice. It was written in the time of the king of kings Khasru Anushirwan.

philosophy.text: In the second half of the sixth century, Arabia yearned for a more spiritual form of religion and began believing in an afterlife. Choosing a religion increasingly became a personal choice rather than a communal one. This happened during a period of political disorder when communication routes were no longer secure.

Some strands of Islamic tradition see the pre-Islamic period as a barbaric, morally un-enlightened age called the "Jahiliyyah". Historians have not adopted this view. They instead treat pre-Islamic Arabia as a region with its own settled and nomadic societies and growing monotheistic religions.

Jewish and Christian ideas changed the way Arabs talked about religion. The old pagan vocabulary of Arabic began to be replaced by Jewish and Christian loanwords from Aramaic everywhere, including Mecca. Although many were reluctant to convert to a foreign faith, those faiths provided intellectual and spiritual reference points.

In the second half of the sixth century, religious divisions were an important cause of Arabia's crisis. Judaism became the dominant religion in Yemen, while Christianity took root in the Persian Gulf area. The period was one of political disorder.

Gerald Hawting argues that Arabian polytheism was marginalized and already dying in Mecca on the eve of Islam. Its practice was increasingly limited to the steppe and the desert. In Yathrib, later known as Medina, no public pagan temple existed in or near the town, which suggests polytheism was confined to the private sphere.

In Arabia the dominant form of Christianity was Miaphysitism, with the exception of Nestorianism in the northeast and around the Persian Gulf. Christian communities were nurtured in northwestern, northeastern and southern Arabia by the influence of the Roman Empire and the Kingdom of Aksum. In other areas Christianity had less presence, though it did win some converts.

In its latest layers, the Quran repeatedly and directly engages with the Mishnah. This likely reflects a growing awareness of, and interaction with, the Jewish scholarly elite. The Quran is an early seventh century source from West Arabia.

Jewish theologians in the late sixth and early seventh centuries wrote polemics defending their religion against Christian and Islamic influences. Judaism was an active proselytising faith at the time, and at least one Arab political leader converted to it.

The Quran mentions Jews and their beliefs often, in both Meccan and Medinan surahs. Jews are mentioned 23 times by the root hwd, 43 times as part of the "Children of Israel", and 32 times as part of the "People of the Book".

The Kaaba in Mecca is said to have contained up to 360 idols. Yet according to some traditions it held no statues at all, and its interior was decorated with images of Mary and Jesus, prophets, angels, and trees. Gerald Hawting has also argued that the Quran's criticism of idolaters is a hyperbolic reference to other monotheists, especially Arab Jews and Arab Christians.

culture.text: In pre-Islamic Arabia, the dominant religious practice was Arab polytheism, centred on local shrines such as the Kaaba in Mecca. Deities were honoured through pilgrimages, divination and ritual sacrifice, including the sacrifice of domestic animals such as camels, sheep and cattle, whose blood was poured out on the altar stone. Human sacrifice was sometimes carried out too, generally of prisoners of war, who represented the god's share of the victory in booty. The Kaaba is said to have contained up to 360 idols.

Arabia in late antiquity was not an isolated backwater. It lay between the Roman or Byzantine, Sasanian and Aksumite empires, and was home to independent kingdoms, oasis communities, nomadic groups and long-distance commercial and religious networks.

Eastern Arabia has a culture that has always been oriented towards the sea, and its people are called Khaleeji, meaning of the Gulf. Seafood forms a major part of the cuisine, and dates are offered to guests alongside Arabic coffee in the majlis.

The Kaaba became a national shrine under the custodianship of the Quraysh, the chief tribe of Mecca. This made the Hejaz the most important religious area in north Arabia. Its environs were regarded as sacred, and within sacred places all living things were considered inviolable and violence was forbidden. Pilgrim fairs took place in months designated as violence-free.

The Christian king Abraha, who controlled much of Arabia from Yemen in the mid-sixth century, built a splendid church in Sanaa and wanted to make it a major pilgrimage centre. Mecca's Kaaba stood in the way of that plan. His attack on Mecca is recounted in Islamic tradition and alluded to in the Quran and pre-Islamic poetry.

Judaism was the first monotheistic religion practised in pre-Islamic Arabia, and Arabian Jews spoke Greek, Aramaic, Arabic and Sabaic. No pre-Islamic translations of Jewish scriptures into Arabian languages have been found, which suggests their religious culture was largely oral.

After Abraha's army was defeated around 565, the Quraysh became a dominant force in western Arabia. Islamic sources say they received the title "God's people" (ahl Allah). They also formed the cult association of ḥums, which tied members of many tribes to the Kaaba.

Gargee'an is a semiannual celebration in Eastern Arabia held on the 15th night of Sha'ban and the 15th night of Ramadan. Children dress in traditional attire and go door-to-door singing songs and receiving sweets from neighbours. The tradition is said to have existed for hundreds of years.

Excavations in Wadi al-Qura at Al-Ula found a late antique village south of ancient Dadan. A large building there was constructed in the late third or early fourth century and used into the first half of the seventh century. It gives rare evidence of settlement, agriculture and diet in northwestern Arabia.

The eighth-century Book of Idols by Hisham ibn al-Kalbi is described by F.E. Peters as the most substantial treatment of the religious practices of pre-Islamic Arabia. Another Muslim source on Arabian beliefs is the Yemeni historian al-Hasan al-Hamdani.
